title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
summary: Fuse ranked lists using only positions: how 1/(k + r) and k decide outliers versus agreement, how RRF compares with CombSUM, Borda and Condorcet, windows, weights, and when score fusion wins.
outcomes: Compute RRF scores by hand for several ranked lists and explain why ranks avoid score calibration
Explain how k trades one system's top hit against agreement between systems
Compare RRF with CombSUM, CombMNZ, Borda count and Condorcet fusion on the same runs
Predict how window size, missing documents, ties and per-list weights change a fused list
Decide when a tuned convex score combination should replace RRF

lessons.title: Why fuse ranks instead of scores

blocks.md: In hybrid search you send one query to two retrievers, BM25 and a dense embedding index, and get back two ranked lists. You now need **one** list. This lesson uses a toy query with six results per list. The BM25 scores are unbounded positive numbers; the dense scores are cosine similarities that sit in a narrow band below 1.

blocks.title: Two result lists for the same query

scenes.caption: BM25 returns D1 to D6 with scores from 18.4 down to 5.0. The dense retriever returns D3, D7, D1, D8, D2, D9 with cosines from 0.86 to 0.70.
Three documents (D1, D2, D3) appear in both lists. These overlaps are what fusion can reward: two independent systems agree on them.
D4, D5, D6 only matched lexically; D7, D8, D9 only matched semantically. A fused list must decide how a one-list document compares with a two-list document.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you just add the raw scores (a document missing from a list adds 0). Where does D7, the dense retriever's second-best hit, end up among the 9 documents?
blocks.reveal: Seventh. Its fused score is 0.84, below every BM25 document (the lowest, D6, has 5.0). The raw sum is the BM25 order with tiny cosine nudges: the dense retriever is effectively ignored because its numbers are on a smaller scale.

blocks.title: Score fusion attempts on the toy lists

scenes.caption: Raw sum. BM25 scores dwarf cosines, so the order is D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6 and only then the dense-only documents.
Min-max normalize each list to [0, 1] first, then add. Better: D1 1.812, D3 1.575, D7 0.875. But D6 and D9 get exactly 0, the same as a document that was never retrieved.

blocks.md: Min-max scaling maps each list's lowest score to 0 and highest to 1, so every normalized value depends on the extremes of **this** query's result list. A single outlier score compresses everything else, and the last retrieved document is indistinguishable from a missing one. Scores also mean different things across queries: a BM25 score of 12 can be the best hit for one query and a weak hit for another.

Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (SIGIR 2009) went the other way: throw the scores away and keep only each document's **rank** (its 1-based position) in each list. They called the result **Reciprocal Rank Fusion** and found it beat the best single system and the established Condorcet fusion on TREC data.

blocks.caption: R is the set of input rankings, r(d) is the rank of document d in ranking r (1 for the top), and k is a constant. Cormack et al. fixed k = 60 in a pilot study.

blocks.md: A document that a list did not return adds nothing for that list (the Elasticsearch pseudocode increments the score only `if d in result(q)`). Every appearance adds at most $1/61 \approx 0.0164$ with $k = 60$. Below, scores are shown multiplied by 1000 to keep the digits readable.

blocks.title: Computing RRF (k = 60) for the toy lists, scores x 1000

scenes.caption: Start with each document's rank in BM25 (B) and in the dense list (D). A dash means the list did not return it.
BM25 contributions 1000/(60 + r): rank 1 gives 16.39, rank 6 gives 15.15. The whole top 6 spans only 1.2 points.
Dense contributions use the same formula on dense ranks. D3 is dense rank 1, so it gets 16.39 there.
Add them. D1 (ranks 1 and 3) and D3 (ranks 3 and 1) tie at 32.27; D2 (2 and 5) is next at 31.51. Every two-list document beats every one-list document.

blocks.md: RRF needs only positions. Scores on different scales, scores that drift between index versions, even systems that expose no scores at all can be fused, because $1/(k + r)$ is the same function of rank for every input.

An RRF score is not a relevance probability. Its size depends on k and on how many lists were fused (Azure AI Search notes each query contributes at most about $1/k$), so do not apply a fixed threshold to it across queries or configurations.

blocks.question: A new BM25 build multiplies every BM25 score by 3 (same order). What happens to the RRF-fused list?
options: Nothing: ranks are unchanged, so every RRF score is unchanged
BM25 now dominates the fusion, like the raw sum
Dense-only documents rise because BM25 is now relatively noisier
The fused list changes only if k is smaller than 3
blocks.explain: RRF reads only r(d). Any monotone transformation of one system's scores leaves its ranks, and therefore the fused list, identical. A raw score sum would change; min-max would not change in this case either, but would under a non-linear transform.

blocks.question: Why do D1 and D3 tie exactly in the toy example?
options: Both have the same BM25 score
Rounding to two decimals hides the difference
Their rank pairs (1, 3) and (3, 1) contain the same ranks, and RRF sums the same terms in a different order
RRF gives every document that appears in two lists the same score
blocks.explain: RRF depends only on the multiset of a document's ranks. 1/61 + 1/63 equals 1/63 + 1/61. D2 is also in two lists but with ranks (2, 5), so it scores lower: two-list documents are not all equal.

lessons.title: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)

blocks.md: Each list turns a rank into a contribution $f(r) = 1/(k + r)$. Only the **relative** sizes of these contributions matter for the final order, so compare every rank with rank 1. That ratio says how much more the top hit is worth than a hit further down.

blocks.caption: With k = 0 rank 1 is worth 10 times rank 10. With k = 10 it is worth 1.82 times, with k = 60 only 1.15 times, with k = 100 about 1.09 times.

blocks.title: Weight of rank r relative to rank 1: (k + 1)/(k + r)

scenes.caption: k = 60, the common default. Rank 10 keeps 87% of rank 1's weight and rank 100 still keeps 38%. The curve is gentle.
k = 0 is plain 1/r (the curve hugs the left edge): rank 2 is worth half of rank 1 and rank 10 a tenth. A single list's top hit dominates.
k = 10: a middle ground. Rank 10 keeps 55% of rank 1's weight.
k = 500: nearly flat. Every retrieved rank is worth almost the same, so fusion mostly counts how many lists returned a document.

blocks.md: Cormack et al. explain the shape: highly ranked documents matter more, but lower ranks should not vanish "as it would were, say, an exponential function used", and the constant k "mitigates the impact of high rankings by outlier systems." The next example makes the outlier effect concrete.

Take two lists. Document X is rank 1 in list A and absent from list B (one enthusiastic system). Document Y is rank 4 in both (two lukewarm systems that agree). X scores $1/(k+1)$ and Y scores $2/(k+4)$. Y wins exactly when $2(k+1) > k+4$, that is when $k > 2$.

blocks.title: Outlier X (rank 1 in one list) versus consensus Y (rank 4 in two)

scenes.caption: At k = 0, X scores 1.0 and Y 0.5: the single system's favorite wins easily.
The curves cross at k = 2, where both score 1/3. For every larger k, agreement beats one strong opinion.

blocks.prompt: At k = 60, document Z is rank 1 in list A and rank 30 in list B. Document W is rank 8 in both. Which ranks higher? What about at k = 0?
blocks.reveal: At k = 60, W wins: $2/68 = 0.0294$ versus $1/61 + 1/90 = 0.0275$. At k = 0, Z wins by a mile: $1 + 1/30 = 1.033$ versus $2/8 = 0.25$. Small k trusts each system's top hits; large k trusts agreement among systems.

blocks.md: Push this further. With k = 60, one appearance is worth between $1/61$ (rank 1) and $1/(60+W)$ at the bottom of a window of W results. A document in $m+1$ lists, even at the worst rank W in each, beats a document in $m$ lists at rank 1 whenever the inequality below holds.

blocks.caption: With k = 60: two-list documents always beat one-list documents if each list returns at most 61 results; three-list beats two-list if each returns at most 31.

blocks.md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

blocks.title: Cormack et al. pilot: MAP of RRF fusing 30 runs, by k

scenes.caption: MAP rises from 0.2072 at k = 0 to a broad plateau of about 0.214 to 0.215 between k = 30 and k = 100, and falls back to 0.2098 at k = 500.
Every k shown beat the best single system in this pilot (MAP 0.2016). The authors concluded k = 60 was near-optimal "but that the choice was not critical."

blocks.md: That pilot fused 30 configurations of one search engine. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023) fused just two systems (BM25 and a dense model) and found NDCG "swings wildly" when they gave each list its own constant, so k is less forgiving in two-list hybrid search than the 2009 plateau suggests. Lesson 6 returns to this.

Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

blocks.question: You raise k from 60 to 600 on a two-list hybrid search. Which description of the new fused order is most accurate?
options: It approaches the BM25 order, because BM25 lists are longer
It approaches ordering by the number of lists that returned each document, with ranks only breaking near-ties
It approaches the order of whichever list has the higher-quality top hit
It is unchanged, because k is added to every rank equally
blocks.explain: Large k flattens 1/(k + r): every appearance is worth nearly 1/k, so documents found by both lists rise above all others and rank differences matter less. Adding k to every rank is not order-preserving after the reciprocal and the sum.

blocks.question: With k = 0 (plain reciprocal rank), what failure do you expect when one of three fused systems is poor?
options: Its rank-1 document gets a full 1.0 and can jump above documents the two good systems both rank 2nd to 3rd
Its documents are ignored because 1/r is too small
Nothing, k only matters for ties
The fused list becomes identical to the poor system's list
blocks.explain: At k = 0, rank 1 gives 1.0 while ranks 2 and 3 in two lists give 0.5 + 0.33 = 0.83. A bad system's favorite can beat documents that two good systems agree on. That is exactly the outlier effect k was chosen to damp.

lessons.title: RRF next to CombSUM, CombMNZ, Borda and Condorcet

blocks.md: Fusing ranked lists is an old problem, called **data fusion** or **metasearch** in the 1990s TREC literature. Cormack et al. built RRF as a simple unsupervised baseline and compared it with these methods, so knowing them shows what RRF keeps and what it drops. We add a third run to the toy: a dense search for an LLM rewrite of the query.

blocks.title: Three runs to fuse (rank 1 on the left)

scenes.caption: Ten distinct documents across three runs. D1, D2, D3 appear in all three. D7 is dense rank 2 and rewrite rank 1, but BM25 never returned it.
D7 (purple) is a strong two-list document. D2 (orange) is in all three lists but low in both dense runs (ranks 5 and 6). Watch where each method puts them.

blocks.md: **Score-based (Fox and Shaw, TREC-2, 1994).** They combined similarity values with CombMAX, CombMIN, CombMED, CombSUM, CombANZ and CombMNZ. CombSUM adds a document's scores across runs. CombMNZ multiplies that sum by the number of runs that returned the document with a nonzero score, explicitly rewarding agreement. Both need scores on comparable scales, so in the toy we min-max normalize each run first.

blocks.caption: s_r(d) is the (normalized) score of d in run r, 0 if r did not return it. Fox and Shaw count nonzero similarities; min-max gives each run's last document 0, so we count runs that returned d, as Cormack et al. define it.

blocks.md:
**Borda count (Aslam and Montague, SIGIR 2001).** Each run is a voter ranking c candidates. The top candidate gets c points, the next c - 1, and so on; candidates a voter left unranked split the remaining points evenly. Here c = 10, so each run's six documents get 10 down to 5 points and the four it missed get 2.5 each.

**Condorcet fusion (Montague and Aslam, CIKM 2002).** For a pair of documents, each run votes for the one it ranks higher (in this toy, an unretrieved document counts as ranked below every retrieved one); the majority wins the pair. Sorting with that comparator yields the fused list in $O(nk \log n)$ time, and documents caught in majority cycles are treated as ties.

blocks.prompt: D7 is rank 2 and 1 in the two dense runs but missing from BM25. D2 is in all three, at ranks 2, 5 and 6. Under RRF with k = 60, which of the two ranks higher? And under the other four methods?
blocks.reveal: RRF puts **D2 third and D7 fourth**: D2 collects three votes of about 1/62 to 1/66, worth 46.67 (x 1000), while D7 collects two, worth 32.52. CombSUM, CombMNZ and Borda all put D7 third and D2 fourth or fifth, and Condorcet even puts D7 second, because two of three runs prefer D7 over D1. This is the vote-counting behavior from lesson 2 in action.

blocks.title: Fused scores for the three runs, method by method

scenes.caption: RRF, k = 60 (x 1000). Three-list documents D3, D1, D2 sit near 47 to 48; two-list D7 and D8 near 32; one-list documents near 15.

CombSUM on min-max scores. The rewrite run's normalized scores (not shown before) are D7 1, D3 0.84, D8 0.58, D1 0.47, D10 0.26, D2 0. D7 (1.875) beats D2 (0.816), whose dense scores sit near each list's minimum.
CombMNZ multiplies by the number of runs: D2 rises to 2.449 (x 3) and passes D8, but D7 (3.75) stays ahead of it.
Borda points. D7 gets 9 + 10 + 2.5 = 21.5, D2 gets 9 + 6 + 5 = 20. The 2.5 consolation points for being unranked keep D7 in the race.
Condorcet: number of pairwise majority contests each document wins. D3 beats all 9 others; D7 beats 8 (everyone but D3), including D1 by 2 runs to 1.

blocks.title: Final fused orders (best on the left)

scenes.caption: All five methods agree that D3 is first. They disagree on D7 (purple) and D2 (orange): RRF is the only one that ranks the three-list D2 above the two-list D7.
Ties: Borda and RRF tie D5 with D10 and D6 with D9 (same points or same rank multiset); Condorcet leaves D6, D9, D10 tied. Tied documents are shown in document-number order.

blocks.md: Which is right? The toy has no relevance labels, so none of them. What the 2009 paper measured: fusing four sets of TREC submissions, RRF's mean average precision (MAP) beat Condorcet in all four and CombMNZ in three; excluding the first pilot (used to choose k), over the other three pilots and the four TREC sets RRF beat Condorcet 7 of 7 times and CombMNZ 6 of 7. On LETOR 3, CombMNZ edged RRF (0.6107 versus 0.6051, p about 0.2, not significant).

blocks.title: Cormack et al. Table 2: MAP when fusing TREC submissions

scenes.caption: TREC 2004 Robust: RRF 0.3686 beats the best submitted run (0.3586), Condorcet (0.3652) and CombMNZ (0.3575).
TREC 3: here CombMNZ (0.4381) edges RRF (0.4350). Both beat the best single run (0.4226).
TREC 5: RRF 0.3394 versus best run 0.3165, the largest gain in the table.
TREC 9: the best run (0.3519) used a human in the loop and beats every fusion. RRF (0.2830) still beats the best automatic run (0.2801).

blocks.md: Cormack et al. point out a practical advantage over Condorcet: RRF needs no voting algorithm or global information, and "ranks may be computed and summed one system at a time", so it streams. Their conjecture for why RRF beats Condorcet: one or two systems that rank a document highly can lift it, whereas "a simple majority of weak preferences may overrule substantially stronger ones."

blocks.question: Which of these methods needs each system's scores, not just its ranks?
options: CombMNZ
Borda count
Condorcet fusion
RRF
blocks.explain: CombSUM and CombMNZ add similarity values (Fox and Shaw combined similarities, typically normalized). Borda, Condorcet and RRF use only the order of each list, which is why they work when scores are missing or incomparable.

blocks.question: You replace every BM25 score by its square root before fusing (same order). Which fused list can change?
options: RRF
Borda
CombSUM on min-max normalized scores
Condorcet
blocks.explain: A square root preserves order, so all rank-based methods are unaffected. Min-max scaling is linear, so after a non-linear transform the normalized values, and therefore the sums, change. Score fusion is sensitive to how scores are shaped, not only to their order.

lessons.title: Ties, missing documents and the window size

blocks.md: Production engines never fuse full rankings of the collection. Each retriever returns its top W results, the **window**: `rank_window_size` per child retriever in Elasticsearch, the `k` of a vector query in Azure AI Search, the set of hits that global-phase reranks in Vespa. A document outside a list's window contributes nothing from that list, exactly as if the list had never matched it.

blocks.title: Fused top results as the window W grows (RRF, k = 60, scores x 1000)

scenes.caption: W = 2. Each list contributes only two documents. D1 and D3 each get one vote (16.39), D2 and D7 one vote each (16.13).
W = 3. D1 (BM25 1, dense 3) and D3 (BM25 3, dense 1) now collect a second vote and jump to 32.27.
W = 4. D4 and D8 enter. D2 is still tied with D7 at 16.13 because D2's dense rank (5) is just outside the window.
W = 6. D2's dense rank 5 now counts: it nearly doubles to 31.51 and pulls clear of D7. One extra window slot changed a document's score by 95%.

blocks.md: Because a second appearance is worth about as much as the first, truncation is a cliff: a document at rank W + 1 in a list gets 0 from it, while rank W gets $1/(k+W)$, almost as much as rank 1. A larger window lets documents just below the cut collect their second vote, at the cost of retrieving and scoring more candidates per list. Elasticsearch requires `rank_window_size` to be at least the page `size`.

Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.

**What should a missing document get?** Three conventions appear in the sources:

1. **Contribute zero** (the RRF formula as Elasticsearch implements it). Equivalent to treating the rank as infinity, the same convention lesson 3 used for the Condorcet toy.
2. **Compute the real rank.** Bruch et al. computed missing scores and ranked documents within the union of candidates. Vespa's global-phase normalizers compute each input for every hit being reranked, so every hit has a rank on every signal.
3. **Penalty rank**, such as W + 1. A shortcut some code uses; it is not in the original paper.

blocks.title: Missing document as zero versus as rank W + 1 = 7 (scores x 1000)

scenes.caption: Zero convention: two-list documents (about 32) sit far above one-list documents (about 15 to 16).
Rank-7 convention: every one-list document gains 1/67 = 14.93 and the gap nearly closes. D7 (31.05) is now within 0.46 of D2 (31.51); with a few more lists, order flips become likely.

blocks.md: **Ties.** RRF ties are common because the score depends only on the multiset of ranks: D1 (1, 3) and D3 (3, 1) tie exactly, as do D4 and D8 (rank 4 in a single list). The pages we read for Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Azure do not document a tie-break rule, so make yours explicit, for example by best single rank, then by document id, so that results are deterministic across pages and replicas. Floating-point addition is not associative, so also sum the lists in a fixed order.

blocks.code:
def rrf(runs, k=60, window=None, weights=None):
    """runs: list of ranked doc-id lists, best first."""
    weights = weights or [1.0] * len(runs)
    score, best = {}, {}
    for w, run in zip(weights, runs):          # fixed list order
        for rank, doc in enumerate(run[:window], start=1):
            score[doc] = score.get(doc, 0.0) + w / (k + rank)
            best[doc] = min(best.get(doc, rank), rank)
    # missing docs contribute 0; ties broken by best rank, then id
    return sorted(score, key=lambda d: (-score[d], best[d], d))

bm25  = ["D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5", "D6"]
dense = ["D3", "D7", "D1", "D8", "D2", "D9"]
print(rrf([bm25, dense], window=4))
# ['D1', 'D3', 'D2', 'D7', 'D4', 'D8']
blocks.caption: A complete RRF with window, weights and a deterministic tie-break. D1 and D3 tie on score and best rank (1), so the id decides.

blocks.question: A product team lowers the per-list window from 50 to 10 to cut latency. Which effect on the fused list should they expect?
options: None, because RRF only looks at the top ranks anyway
Documents ranked 11 to 50 in one list lose that vote entirely, so some documents that both lists liked moderately drop below documents only one list returned
All RRF scores shrink by the same factor, so the order is unchanged
Ties disappear
blocks.explain: Each appearance in a window is worth roughly the same at k = 60, so losing a vote is a big change. A document at ranks 3 and 20 had two votes with W = 50 but has one with W = 10.

blocks.question: Your fused results flicker between two orders on repeated identical requests. Which fix addresses the most likely cause?
options: Increase k
Add an explicit tie-break (best single rank, then document id) after sorting by RRF score
Normalize scores with min-max before RRF
Switch to CombSUM
blocks.explain: Exact RRF ties are frequent (any two documents with the same multiset of ranks). Without an explicit secondary key their order depends on hash or arrival order. Changing k changes which documents tie but does not remove ties.

blocks.md: Plain RRF trusts every list equally. When you know one retriever is better for your traffic, **weighted RRF** multiplies each list's contribution by a weight $w_r$. Search engines expose this directly.

blocks.caption: Only the ratios between weights matter: multiplying all weights by the same constant scales every score equally and leaves the order unchanged.

blocks.md:
- **Elasticsearch** `rrf` retriever: an optional per-child `weight` (default 1.0, non-negative) that multiplies that retriever's contribution; `rank_constant` defaults to 60.
- **OpenSearch** `score-ranker-processor`: `combination.parameters.weights`, one value in [0, 1] per query clause, summing to 1.0; `rank_constant` in [1, 10000], default 60.
- **Azure AI Search**: a vector query `weight` multiplies that query's reciprocal-rank score before summing (default 1.0).
- **Vespa**: `reciprocal_rank(f, k)` (k defaults to 60) is an ordinary ranking-expression term in global-phase, and `reciprocal_rank_fusion(a, b)` is shorthand for their sum, so weights are just multipliers you write.

blocks.title: Weighted RRF on the two-list toy (k = 60, scores x 1000)

scenes.caption: Weights (1, 1): plain RRF. Two-list documents near 32, then one-list documents ordered by their single rank.
BM25 1, dense 1.5. D3 (dense rank 1) now leads D1. Dense-only D9 (rank 6, 22.73) passes BM25-only D4 (rank 4, 15.62).
BM25 2, dense 1. The mirror image: D1 leads and all BM25-only documents (about 30) beat all dense-only ones (about 15).
OpenSearch-style weights (0.7, 0.3). Same ratio as (2.33, 1), so the order matches a BM25-heavy weighting; only the score scale differs.

blocks.md: A weight acts on whole votes. Because every rank in a window is worth nearly $1/k$ at k = 60, a weight of 1.5 mostly decides **which list's single-list documents come first**, and only lightly reorders documents both lists returned. That is a blunter tool than tuning α in a score combination.

Bruch et al. point out a second, hidden knob: give each list its own constant, $1/(k_{\text{lex}} + r) + 1/(k_{\text{sem}} + r)$. A larger constant flattens (discounts) that list. On the toy, $(k_{\text{lex}}, k_{\text{sem}}) = (10, 4)$ makes the dense list steep: D3 leads D1 by 276.9 to 233.8 (x 1000) and dense-only D7 (166.7) jumps above all BM25-only documents. In their experiments, the (10, 4) setting tuned on in-domain data raised MS MARCO NDCG@1000 from 0.425 to 0.451 but cut HotpotQA from 0.675 to 0.621.

blocks.prompt: OpenSearch requires weights that sum to 1, such as (0.7, 0.3). Elasticsearch takes any non-negative weights. Does Elasticsearch with weights (7, 3) produce the same fused order as OpenSearch with (0.7, 0.3), given the same k and lists?
blocks.reveal: Yes. Every score is multiplied by 10, which preserves the order. Only the ratio $w_1 / w_2$ matters, so (0.7, 0.3), (7, 3) and (2.33, 1) are interchangeable for ranking. The absolute score values differ, which matters only if something downstream reads them.

blocks.md: **Multi-query fusion.** RRF is not limited to different retrievers. **RAG-Fusion**, popularized by Adrian Raudaschl, asks an LLM to rewrite the user's question into several queries, runs a search for each, fuses the result lists with RRF, and passes the fused documents to the LLM to answer. Rackauckas (2024) evaluated it in a product-information chatbot at Infineon.

scenes.caption: The user question goes to an LLM, which writes several related queries (the reference repo asks for 4).
Each query runs its own vector search and returns a ranked list.
RRF fuses the per-query lists into one ranking; documents that many rewrites retrieve rise to the top.
The fused documents plus the queries go to the LLM for the answer. This second, larger LLM call dominated the extra latency in the Infineon study.
Four rewrites, five passages each. Query 4 drifted: its top hit P9 appears in no other list.
P2 (ranks 1, 3, 1, 2) and P1 (2, 1, 3, 4) appear in all four lists and score 64.79 and 64.02 (x 1000). Two-list passages P5, P6, P4, P3 follow at about 31 to 32.
P9 was rank 1 for query 4 but lands 7th with 16.39. A single drifting rewrite cannot push its favorite to the top; the flip side is that one uniquely good rewrite cannot either.

blocks.md: Multi-query fusion has costs. In the Infineon study RAG-Fusion averaged 34.62 s versus 19.52 s for plain RAG (1.77 times slower in that deployment), mostly from the larger answer call, and some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough. If the rewrites are near-duplicates, fusion just re-counts the same list.

blocks.question: In a hybrid setup the dense retriever is clearly better on your traffic. You set Elasticsearch weights BM25 = 1, dense = 3 with k = 60. What is the main effect?
options: Dense-only documents move above BM25-only documents, while documents both lists return stay on top
BM25 is ignored completely
The fused order is unchanged because RRF ignores weights when k = 60
Documents both lists return drop below dense-only documents
blocks.explain: A two-list document gets about (1 + 3)/61 at best and (1 + 3)/(60 + W) at worst, while a dense-only document gets at most 3/61, so agreement still wins as long as each window holds at most 21 results (4/(60 + W) > 3/61). The weight mainly reorders single-list documents and nudges the order among two-list ones.

blocks.question: Why does a single off-topic rewrite in RAG-Fusion usually do limited damage to the fused list?
options: RRF detects off-topic queries and drops them
RRF uses the cosine scores, which are lower for off-topic results
Its documents get at most one vote of about 1/61, while documents shared by several rewrites collect several votes
The LLM answer step re-sorts documents by relevance
blocks.explain: RRF knows nothing about topicality. The protection is structural: a document returned by only one of four lists can reach about 1/61, while documents several lists agree on get two to four votes. The same mechanism also buries a uniquely good rewrite's finds.

blocks.md: RRF's strength, ignoring scores, is also its weakness. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (ACM TOIS 2023) compared it with a **convex combination** (CC) of normalized scores on BM25 plus a dense model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) across MS MARCO and eight BEIR datasets.

blocks.caption: TM2C2 is CC with theoretical min-max scaling: the floor is the score's smallest possible value (0 for BM25, -1 for cosine), not the smallest score in this list.

blocks.md: Consider a query where BM25 barely separates its hits (11.9, 11.7, 11.6, 11.4 for A, B, C, E) but the dense model has one clear winner: C at 0.91, then A 0.52, B 0.51, F 0.50. The ranks are BM25 (A, B, C, E) and dense (C, A, B, F).

blocks.prompt: Under RRF (k = 60), which document is first: A (ranks 1 and 2) or C (ranks 3 and 1)? And under CC with α = 0.8?
blocks.reveal: RRF puts **A** first: $1/61 + 1/62 = 0.03252$ versus $1/63 + 1/61 = 0.03227$. CC puts **C** first (0.995 versus 0.837), because C's dense lead (0.91 versus 0.52) is large while A's BM25 lead (11.9 versus 11.6) is tiny. RRF sees only that A beats C in one list and C beats A in the other.

scenes.caption: RRF (x 1000). A 32.52 edges C 32.27: RRF cannot tell a 0.39 cosine gap from a 0.01 gap.
CC with tmm scaling, α = 0.8. C gets 0.995, far ahead of A (0.837): the dense model's confidence carries through.
Now shrink C's cosine to 0.525, still rank 1. It becomes the dense max, so A's normalized cosine jumps: A 0.997 now edges C 0.995. RRF's scores are exactly the same as in the first scene.

blocks.md: Simplified: in this toy a document missing from a list adds 0 on that side; Bruch et al. compute the real missing score instead. Their formal point is that RRF is not Lipschitz continuous in the scores: a tiny score change that swaps two ranks causes a jump, while a huge score change that keeps ranks does nothing. A smoothed RRF (SRRF) that softens this jump often scored higher than RRF in their experiments.

blocks.title: Bruch et al. Table 3: NDCG@1000, TM2C2 (α = 0.8) versus RRF variants

scenes.caption: MS MARCO (in-domain for the dense model). TM2C2 0.454 beats RRF(60, 60) 0.425. RRF tuned to (10, 4) almost catches up at 0.451.
NQ (in-domain). TM2C2 0.542, RRF(60, 60) 0.514; the tuned (10, 4) reaches 0.528.
HotpotQA (out-of-domain). TM2C2 0.699, RRF(60, 60) 0.675, and the in-domain-tuned RRF(10, 4) collapses to 0.621.
FEVER (out-of-domain). Same pattern: 0.744, 0.721, 0.727, and 0.649 for the tuned RRF.
FiQA (out-of-domain). TM2C2 0.496 versus RRF(60, 60) 0.464. TM2C2 beat default RRF on all nine datasets in the table.

blocks.md: Two more findings matter for practice. Tuning α is **sample-efficient**: with under 5% of each training set, often a small set of queries, TM2C2's α converged regardless of domain shift. And the choice of normalization (min-max, z-score, theoretical min-max) mattered little once α was tuned, but **some** normalization was essential: adding unnormalized BM25 to cosine scores badly hurt in-domain quality.

RRF trades information for robustness: it ignores how far apart scores are, so it cannot be fooled by scale, but it also cannot use a confident gap. With labels and comparable scores, a tuned convex combination usually wins; without them, RRF is the safe default.

Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

blocks.question: An internal search fuses BM25 with a dense model. You have 300 labeled queries from real traffic, and both retrievers expose stable scores. What does the evidence suggest?
options: Keep RRF with k = 60; tuning anything overfits
Tune a convex combination of normalized scores (one α) and compare it against RRF on held-out queries
Tune separate RRF constants per list, since that has more parameters
Use CombMAX, since it keeps the best score
blocks.explain: Bruch et al. found a convex combination with one tuned α beat RRF in and out of domain and converged with few labeled queries. Per-list RRF constants helped in-domain but generalized poorly. Always confirm on held-out data.

blocks.question: Which situation most favors RRF over score fusion?
options: Both systems return calibrated probabilities of relevance
One input is a third-party search API that returns only an ordered list of URLs
The dense model often has one very confident top hit far above the rest
You have thousands of labeled queries and a stable index
blocks.explain: With no scores at all, rank fusion is the natural option. Calibrated probabilities, confident score gaps and plenty of labels are all cases where score information helps and a convex combination tends to do better.
